title: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do

fields.label: Label
fields.value: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: from experience in practical computing one knows that it is usually very difficult to foresee what even a simple program will do.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 2, “The Crucial Experiment”; section “Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before” (from p. 42), p. 46. Scope: simple programs, including software and cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch02-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public software and bug benchmarks allow limited prediction and defect analyses. They are biased toward larger real projects and do not represent all simple programs, so the general prevalence claim remains partial.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample programs under a declared simplicity measure and compare human or automated predictions of behavior with actual runs; separately measure defect rates by program complexity. High error for simple programs and an association with bugs would support the operationalized version.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Source-code simplicity is encoding-dependent.

Usually depends on an unspecified program distribution.

Bug frequency has many causes besides behavioral unpredictability.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data existence: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The working content is a performance claim about prediction of simple programs, and a blinded comparison of non-simulating predictors with direct runs is a standard analysis on public rule families. Adequacy is limited by the open-ended population of 'simple programs,' which a stratified sample still represents at the strength the word 'usually' requires. The appeal to software bugs is illustrative and is not needed for the test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample short programs and elementary cellular automata, and score predictors that do not simulate (closed forms, static inspection, small statistical models) against the true trajectories. The claim is confirmed if accuracy is low for most of the sample, and refuted if a cheap predictor usually matches the run.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Usually and simple need explicit cutoffs.

Software-bug anecdotes are a separate, poorly standardized empirical clause.

A predictor that secretly simulates the program would make the test vacuous.
